title: Ìlèkè Ẹsẹ̀
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí a bá ń ròyìn ìlèkè ẹsẹ̀, a máa ń fi ẹsẹ̀ sẹ́yìn. (When reciting the grandeur of royal ankle beads, one steps backward in humble deference; dignity and noble presence demand measured movement.)

Saworo ẹsẹ̀ kì í dákẹ́ láì fọhùn, ẹni gbé ìlèkè wọ̀ gbọdọ̀ tẹ ilẹ̀ pẹ̀lú ọgbọ́n. (The chiming bells upon the ankle never stay silent; whoever wears sacred beads must tread upon the earth with wisdom: Every step carries moral consequence.)

Ẹsẹ̀ tí kò wọ ìlèkè kì í mọ iyì ijó; àkún ẹsẹ̀ ló ń bu ọlá fún ìrìn aláyé. (The ankle that wears no beads knows not the dignity of the sacred dance; it is the beaded anklet that confers grace upon the sovereign stride: Dignified bearing honors ancestral presence.)
provenance_and_citations: Drewal, Henry John, & Pemberton, John III (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought. New York: Center for African Art; Eicher, Joanne Bubolz (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles. Ile-Ife: University of Ife Press; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gẹ̀lẹ̀dẹ́ Spectacle. Seattle: University of Washington Press.

title: Fìlà Abetí Ajá
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Fìlà kì í ṣe orí, aṣọ lásán ni a fi ń ṣe é; ṣùgbọ́n bí ó bá bà lé orí tán, ó di ọlá. (A cap is not the head itself, for it is fashioned from simple cloth; yet when placed upon the head, it transforms into an emblem of honor: Form and decorum elevate ordinary humanity.)

Bí a bá wọ fìlà abetí ajá, a kì í fẹ́ kí ẹlòmíràn bá ni tẹ́ etí rẹ̀. (If a person wears the dog-eared cap, they brook no stranger adjusting its flaps; personal sovereignty and sartorial dignity remain in the custody of the wearer.)

Etí fìlà abetí ajá kì í gbọ́ ọ̀rọ̀ èké; ibi tí ọlọ́gbọ́n bá dárí rẹ̀ sí ni ó ń kọjú sí. (The flaps of the dog-eared cap never heed falsehood; wherever the wise person directs them is where they face: Non-verbal sartorial expression signals inner discernment.)
provenance_and_citations: Eicher, Joanne Bubolz (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles. Ile-Ife: University of Ife Press; Nwafor, Okechukwu (2021). Aso Ebi: Cloth and Sociability in Urban Nigeria. Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press; Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba. Ibadan: Ibadan University Press.

title: Fìlà Ọ̀ránmíyàn
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Orí tí yóò wọ adé Ọ̀ránmíyàn kì í ṣe orí alápatà (The head destined to wear the tall martial crown of Ọ̀ránmíyàn cannot be that of a common merchant; regal authority demands imperial destiny and heroic sacrifice.)

Bí fìlà bá gùn tó Ọ̀ránmíyàn, kí ọmọdé mọ̀ pé ogun ló bi í (If a cap rises as tall as the column of Ọ̀ránmíyàn, the youth must recognize that war forged its foundation: Dynastic grandeur is paid for in battle.)

Ọ̀ránmíyàn sọkò, fìlà rẹ̀ fìdí kalẹ̀; ẹni tí ń wọ aṣọ akọni kì í sá lójú ogun. (Ọ̀ránmíyàn anchored his reign, and his tall crown stood firm; he who wears the attire of the conqueror never flees from conflict: Imperial ancestry demands valor.)
provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Eicher, Joanne Bubolz (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles. Ile-Ife: University of Ife Press; Smith, Robert S. (1988). Kingdoms of the Yoruba. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.

title: Pà Kaja
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí a bá fi aṣọ pà kàjà, a máa ń múra sí iṣẹ́ ni. (When one slaps the cloth across the shoulder, it signifies active readiness for labor; garments folded across the torso prepare the body for disciplined exertion.)

Ẹni tí ó pà kàjà tí kò mọ ọ̀nà ogun, yóò fi aṣọ rèé gbá koríko lójú pápá. (He who folds his cloth across the chest without military discipline will merely drag his mantle through the dust: Outer preparedness without inner resolve brings mockery.)

A kì í pà kàjà láì múra sí àgbájọ ọwọ́; aṣọ tí a wọ mọ́ra ló ń sọ ìgboyà ọkùnrin di àṣẹ. (One does not drape the mantle crosswise without girding oneself for action; the cloth slung across the torso turns courage into command: Martial readiness demands mental focus.)
provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Ajayi, J. F. A., & Smith, Robert S. (1964). Yoruba Warfare in the Nineteenth Century. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press; Eicher, Joanne Bubolz (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles. Ile-Ife: University of Ife Press.

title: Ọ̀pá Ọ̀rànmíyàn
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀pá tí a fi ń ṣọ́ọ̀lú, kì í ṣé kó sẹ́yìn (The staff used to guard the township never breaks or retreats; ancestral protection stands unwavering against external threat.)
Ọ̀rànmíyàn sọkò mọ́lẹ̀, ó di òkúta àìgbégbé (Ọ̀rànmíyàn drove his spear into the earth, and it became an unshakeable megalith; dynastic legitimacy is carved into the eternal rock of the homeland.)

Ọ̀pá Ọ̀ránmíyàn kì í wó sọ́tùn-ún, bẹ́ẹ̀ ni kì í wó sósì; ààrin gbùngbùn Ilé-Ifẹ̀ ló fìdí kalẹ̀ sí. (The staff of Ọ̀rànmíyàn never tilts to the right, nor does it fall to the left; it stands rooted at the very epicenter of Ilé-Ifẹ̀: Ancestral sovereignty remains immovable.)
provenance_and_citations: Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas. London: Routledge; Willett, Frank (1967). Ife in the History of West African Sculpture. London: Thames and Hudson; Smith, Robert S. (1988). Kingdoms of the Yoruba. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.

title: Èwù Ìlèkè
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Bí a bá fi èwù ìlèkè ṣe àṣọ, a kì í ṣègbé e lórí pátápátá; ọlá tó dán mọ́ràn kò ṣeé fi fún ẹnikẹ́ni. (When a beaded garment is worn, it is never handled lightly; resplendent royal honor cannot be surrendered to the profane.)

Ọba tó wọ èwù ìlèkè ti wọ agbára ilẹ̀ mọ́ra; ara rẹ̀ kì í ṣe ara lásán mọ́. (The King who dons the beaded tunic has enveloped himself in the power of the sacred Earth; his mortal body becomes an altar of collective destiny.)

Ọba tó wọ èwù ìlèkè kò gbọdọ̀ tẹrí gba àbùkù; gbogbo ara rẹ̀ ló ti di àṣẹ àti ẹ̀ṣọ́ orílẹ̀. (The King who dons the beaded tunic must never succumb to dishonor; his entire being has become the embodiment of divine authority and national beauty: Royal adornment is a sacred trust.)
provenance_and_citations: Drewal, Henry John, & Pemberton, John III (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought. New York: Center for African Art; Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press; Eicher, Joanne Bubolz (1976). Nigerian Handcrafted Textiles. Ile-Ife: University of Ife Press.

title: Ọ̀pá Àṣẹ
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀pá tí kò ní àṣẹ, kì í ṣe àkúnya; ẹnu tí kò ní ọ̀rọ̀ àṣẹ kì í sọ̀rọ̀ di dandan. (A staff lacking spiritual authority is merely a piece of wood; a mouth without the command of truth cannot speak words into irrevocable existence.)

Bí Ọba bá ti fi Ọ̀pá Àṣẹ tẹ ilẹ̀, ọ̀rọ̀ ti parí sí orí àwọn aláyé. (When the King strikes the ground with the scepter of command, the verdict is sealed across the terrestrial realm: Sovereign judgment is final.)

Ọ̀pá Àṣẹ kì í dákẹ́ bí Ọba bá fọhùn; àṣẹ tí a fi tẹ ilẹ̀ kò ní yípadà títí ayé. (The scepter of command is never mute when the King speaks; the decree stamped into the earth shall never be undone: Cosmic authority seals divine justice.)
provenance_and_citations: Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language: Seeking the African in African Art. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press; Drewal, Henry John, & Pemberton, John III (1989). Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought. New York: Center for African Art; Ìdòwú, E. Bọ́lájì (1962). Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief. London: Longmans.
